name: Fused Relative NP

1.definition: Identifies a person, thing, or quantity through the relation expressed inside the NP.
1.details: In what she wrote, the initial expression supplies both the nominal reference and a dependent of wrote. The resulting NP can denote written material. The same word sequence can form an embedded interrogative about the identity of that material. In subject position a plural fused relative licenses plural agreement, whereas a clausal subject takes default singular agreement.

examples.note: Fused relative contrasted with the interrogative after wonder.

examples.form: [What books she has] are in the attic.
examples.note: The NP has plural agreement despite containing a finite clause.

relatedConstructions.notes: The whole expression distributes as an NP.
A relative expression helps identify the nominal referent.
The same string can express an embedded question in another construction.
The variable expression of a pseudo-cleft is a fused relative.

projection.target: Identical-looking subordinate strings can differ in agreement and complement distribution. A plural fused relative can control plural agreement where an open interrogative cannot.
projection.evidence: CGEL uses agreement, extraposition and selection as diagnostics independent of the referential contrast. The NP is also the variable expression in the CASA wh-cleft.

curious.title: A what phrase that acts as a noun phrase
curious.summary: A phrase like what she wrote names the thing that was written, much as a noun phrase would.
curious.body:
In I really liked what she wrote, the phrase what she wrote names the thing that was written. The word what does two jobs: it supplies the thing referred to, and it fills the place after wrote where that thing would go.

The same words can instead be a question about identity, as after wonder. One clue to the difference is the verb. In What books she has are in the attic, the phrase takes the plural are, where a clause on its own as subject would take a singular verb.

examples.text: [What books she has] are in the attic.

curious.try: Compare I really liked what she wrote with I wonder what she wrote. In which one is what she wrote a thing you could point at?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: what she wrote as a noun phrase, and how it differs from an embedded question.
teacher.explain: A fused relative NP identifies a person, thing or quantity through the relation expressed inside the NP. In what she wrote, the initial expression supplies both the nominal reference and a dependent of wrote, so the NP can denote written material. The same string can form an embedded interrogative about the identity of the material. Diagnostics independent of the referential contrast include agreement, extraposition and selection: a plural fused relative as subject licenses plural agreement (What books she has are in the attic), whereas a clausal subject takes default singular agreement. The variable expression of a pseudo-cleft is a fused relative. Confidence in this dictionary is high.
teacher.terms: Fused relative is CGEL's term. Free relative and nominal relative are sometimes used for the same thing.

examples.text: [What books she has] are in the attic.

contrasts.text: I really liked what she wrote.
contrasts.note: Fused relative; the NP denotes written material.
The same words as an embedded question about identity.

watch_for: A learner might read what she wrote in I really liked what she wrote as a question.
A learner might choose a singular verb after What books she has, because the phrase contains a finite clause.
teacher.activity: Students get pairs like I liked what she wrote and I wonder what she wrote. They decide which is a noun phrase naming something and which is a question. They can check by the verb: What books she has are in the attic.
